questions.question: What two specific fears about Allah's relationship with the Prophet does verse 3 directly negate?
options: Fear of poverty and fear of weakness
Fear of abandonment and fear of divine displeasure
Fear of mockery and fear of military defeat
Fear of doubt and fear of forgetting revelation
questions.explanation: Allah negates 'wadda'a' (taking leave or abandoning) and 'qala' (becoming displeased or hateful), addressing both the external concern that revelation had stopped and the internal fear that the Prophet had somehow caused divine displeasure.

questions.question: True or false: Surah Ad-Duha was revealed during a period when revelation had paused (the fatra), and some among the Quraysh were mocking the Prophet by saying his Lord had abandoned him.
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that the surah was revealed at a time of immense emotional distress for the Prophet, when an extended pause in revelation led some among the Quraysh to claim that his Lord had abandoned him or grown displeased.

questions.question: What does verse 4 ('And the Hereafter is better for you than the first life') establish as a core Islamic orientation?
options: That this world is wicked and must be entirely abandoned
That worldly success is the true measure of divine favor
That the Hereafter is categorically superior to this transient first life
That suffering in this world guarantees salvation in the next
questions.explanation: The verse uses 'al-ula' (the first) rather than 'al-dunya,' framing this life simply as what comes first temporally. It establishes that the Hereafter is decisively superior in duration, pleasure, peace, and nearness to Allah.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 5 promises a specific enumerated list of blessings to the Prophet, naming exactly what Allah will give.
questions.explanation: The verse is deliberately open-ended. The tafsir explains that it does not enumerate because the scope of divine giving cannot be contained in a list; the test of sufficiency is the Prophet's own complete satisfaction (fatarda).

questions.question: According to Ibn Kathir, what did the Prophet say that revealed how he understood the promise of verse 5?
options: 'I will be satisfied only when Mecca is conquered'
'I will not be pleased while even one of my ummah remains in the Fire'
'I am already satisfied with what my Lord has given me'
'My satisfaction lies only in the wealth of this world'
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir cites the narration in Sahih Muslim where the Prophet, on hearing this verse, said he would not be pleased while even one of his ummah remained in the Fire, indicating that the divine promise includes his intercession (shafa'ah) for his community.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir and other classical Sunni scholars interpret 'dallan' in verse 7 to mean that the Prophet was a polytheist or in moral error before revelation.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir explicitly explains that 'dallan' does not mean the Prophet was misguided or followed falsehood, as this would contradict his prophetic purity. Rather, it means he was unaware of the detailed injunctions of Islamic law and the full content of revelation before it was sent down.

questions.question: How does Imam al-Qurtubi in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran extend the prohibition 'do not oppress the orphan' (la taqhar)?
options: He limits it to physical violence only
He restricts it to a guardian's direct biological relatives
He extends it to taking their property, delaying inheritance, and harsh speech or action
He applies it only to Meccan orphans during the Prophet's lifetime
questions.explanation: Al-Qurtubi extracts from this verse a broad prohibition covering eating orphans' property, delaying their inheritance, forcing them into undesirable situations, and treating them harshly in speech or action, connecting it to the wider fiqh in Surah al-Nisa and al-Baqarah.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli explains that the command not to repel the petitioner (sa'il) is grounded in the Islamic concept of human dignity (karamah), and applies to those seeking knowledge as well as material help.
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir connects the verse to the concept of karamah, noting that every petitioner, whether asking for material help or guidance, carries an inherent dignity that must not be violated. Ibn Kathir likewise affirms that 'al-sa'il' encompasses both the beggar and the seeker of knowledge.

questions.question: According to Sayyid Qutb's reading in Fi Zilal al-Quran, how do verses 9, 10, and 11 relate to the divine favors mentioned in verses 6, 7, and 8?
options: They are unrelated commands placed at the end for emphasis
They abrogate the earlier verses about the Prophet's history
They form a symmetrical response: each remembered favor produces a corresponding moral imperative
They apply only to the Prophet personally and not to his community
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb highlights the symmetry: orphanhood is answered by protecting the orphan, lostness by welcoming the seeker, and poverty by proclaiming divine favor. Ethics in Islam flow organically from remembered experience and gratitude rather than abstract obligation.
